segments.text: Seventeen days after a mine collapses, a drill comes back up out of the ground, with a note tied to it.
A note? From seven hundred metres down? No chance. Let's go look.
In red ink, it says: we are fine in the shelter, the thirty-three of us.

Go back seventeen days. The fifth of August, {2010|twenty ten}. The San José mine, in Chile's Atacama desert. Copper and gold, and more than a century of digging. Thirty-three men are deep inside, on their shift.
Then the mountain comes down. Rock seals the only road out, and for hours the dust is so thick the men can barely see.
There is one other way out: a ventilation shaft. It is supposed to have a ladder, all the way to the surface. The ladder was never finished.
So they go down instead, to the emergency shelter, seven hundred metres under the desert. And they open the food locker.
It holds food for about two days. They vote on everything, and they vote for this. Each man gets two spoonfuls of tuna, a sip of milk and a bite of cracker. Every other day.
It is hot down there, and wet. They drink water drained from the machines, and run their helmet lamps off truck batteries. I'd have complained. Loudly.
Up top, their families camp at the mine gate, and will not leave. They call it Camp Hope. And the drills start down, through seven hundred metres of rock, aimed at one small room.
One after another, they miss. Seven holes. And nobody on the surface knows if anyone down there is still alive.
Day seventeen. The eighth drill comes through the roof, close to the shelter. And the men tie a note to it.
That's the note. Thirty-three men, all alive. The whole camp goes wild. So did I.
But now comes the hard part. That hole fits a note. It does not fit a man. And the first estimate for getting them out is four months.
So the little hole becomes a lifeline. Down it go narrow tubes the rescuers call doves, carrying glucose and medicine, then food. And letters from home. Even a video camera.
Meanwhile, three drills race each other down. Plan A. Plan B. Plan C. Below, the miners work in shifts, clearing the rock that falls as the new shaft is cut.
On the ninth of October, Plan B breaks through. A shaft more than six hundred metres long, and about as wide as a bicycle wheel.
The navy builds a steel capsule to ride in it. Fifty-four centimetres across. Barely wider than a man's shoulders. I tried one. Don't.
And the first person to ride it goes the wrong way. A rescuer, Manuel González, goes down alone, to get the men ready.
Then, around midnight, the first miner starts up. One man, in the dark, through solid rock.
Just after midnight, on the thirteenth of October, he steps out, in dark glasses against the lights. The second man up brings rocks from the mine, as souvenirs. My kind of miner.
They come up one at a time, all night and all day. Twenty-two hours later, the count is thirty-three out of thirty-three. Sixty-nine days underground.
The last miner out is their foreman, Luis Urzúa. Then the rescuers ride up. The very last is Manuel González, the man who went down first. And the mine is empty.
A lid goes over the shaft. Prosecutors closed the case in {2013|twenty thirteen}, and nobody was charged. But every one of those men came back up into the light.
I said no chance. I was wrong. Case closed.
